text: Chapter two. Is the crowd really the enemy, or is that just snobbery? Samuel, you opened with that, so make your case properly.

speaker: Guest2
text: Gladly. Adorno wrote a whole book about this, The Jargon of Authenticity, from 1964. I'll paraphrase, because the argument matters more than the phrasing. He noticed that post-war Germany was full of a certain elevated vocabulary. Words like authenticity, encounter, commitment, the genuine. They were used by philosophers, by preachers, by teachers and by politicians, and they made people sound deep without saying anything checkable. Heidegger was his main philosophical target. And one of Adorno's charges is that the contempt for the everyday "they" has an elitist tone. The philosopher stands above the crowd and diagnoses it.

speaker: Guest
text: I know the book, and I'll defend Heidegger on the snobbery charge directly, because he saw it coming. speaker: Guest2
text: Saying "I'm not moralizing" doesn't stop you moralizing. If I call you lazy and then add "no offence", I've still called you lazy. He chooses words like idle talk, curiosity, falling, uprooted, a downward plunge. Those aren't neutral lab terms.

speaker: Guest
text: Fair, the vocabulary is loaded. I'll concede that. In German some of those words sound even harsher. But look at what he does with the crowd. He never says there's an elite that escapes it. speaker: Host
text: So nobody gets a VIP pass. Not even the philosopher.

speaker: Guest
text: Not even the philosopher. He's in the they too. That's the opposite of elitism. Everyone starts from the same place, including him.

speaker: Guest2
text: That's a better reading than most people give him, I'll grant it. But here's Adorno's deeper point. Even if Heidegger's in the crowd with us, he describes the crowd as a timeless feature of being human. Adorno says that's exactly the problem. The pressure to conform in a modern office, a modern city, a modern media market, is produced by history, by economics, by how work is organised. Make it eternal, and you've taken it out of the reach of politics. You can't reform an existentiale.

speaker: Guest
text: Except Heidegger says, in so many words, that the dominion of the they may change in the course of history. He leaves the door open.
